Then, on July 14, Trump announced that he was withdrawing the fee proposal and replacing it with trade and investment deals that Gulf countries would make with the United States. He said the decision was based on talks with Middle Eastern leaders. The headline changed from a fee plan to trade and investment deals.

One might have thought the market would catch its breath too, but the story did not end there. After the announcement, Brent crude futures, an international benchmark, briefly gave back some of their gains. But soon they returned to a level close to where they had been before the announcement. At the time of the report, they were above $85 a barrel, up about 2.6 percent.

This price move alone does not show that the market felt reassured by the withdrawal, or that the proposal meant nothing. At the time, attacks by the United States and Iran and a sea blockade continued, and concerns about tanker safety remained. Nor can this price move alone tell us how replacing the plan with trade and investment deals affected ship safety.
